extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and academic authors preparing mathematical documents (papers, books, lectures)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, editing, typesetting, and publishing mathematical documents—covering backups, editors, word processors, TeX, graphics, spell-checking, hypertext, and Open Access considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep old versions / save drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep all the old versions; every draft of every one of your works will only take up a small fraction of your hard disc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having old versions available is psychologically helpful and allows resuscitating old turns of phrase. When work is complete you may discard drafts except the final one, but storage is cheap so retain versions until sure. Example: author discarded >1300 bytes resulting in version 005 — old versions can be useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular backups (modified Tower of Hanoi protocol)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the habit of doing regular backups. The 'by the book' method for doing backups is the 'modified Tower of Hanoi' protocol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At minimum, back up all critical files to an external hard drive, flash drive, or other mass storage at least once per week. Backups protect against catastrophic loss (e.g., losing your C: drive is like your house burning down).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cloud backups as extra security
rubrics_metrics.description: These days it is a good yoga to back up your files to the cloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cloud is somebody else's hard drive — well-maintained and accessible from anywhere — and provides extra security for your data. Treat cloud as complement, not sole absolute guarantee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a first-rate text editor for authoring
rubrics_metrics.description: If you do your writing with a first-rate text editor, then you have powerful tools at your disposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good editors let you open several files and portions at once, integrate bibliographic resource files, and switch quickly between tools (dictionary, thesaurus, Internet). Using technology avoids interruptions to thought processes and creative flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Print drafts and proofread on paper
rubrics_metrics.description: After writing a draft, print it out, lounge in your most comfortable chair, and proofread and edit with a red pen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper copy stimulates critical thinking; some authors prefer editing on paper rather than on-screen. Decide what works for you. Beware that typeset printed output can look falsely final—retrain yourself to read typeset work critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the 'finished' look of typeset output
rubrics_metrics.description: When the MS is typeset, the product looks like a finished product which makes it more difficult to see present flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even handwritten copy can hide structure problems; after typesetting, actively seek paragraphs that must be rearranged or rewritten. Don't let polished appearance prevent further improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word processor advantages (features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Word processor performs many useful functions: automatic line wrap, easy insert/delete/move of text, right justification, spell checking, printer communication (WYSIWYG), incorporate graphics, global search-and-replace, multiple fonts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features save time and are why most professional people prepare documents on a word processor. Examples: change a mapping name across whole paper with search-and-replace; WYSIWYG for print-preview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word processor limitations for mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: From the point of view of a mathematician, a word processor is not entirely satisfactory: it will not typeset mathematics in an acceptable fashion or treat complicated mathematical expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word processors struggle with commutative diagrams, matrices of matrices, combined superscripts/subscripts, delicate kerning and spacing; WYSIWYG is limited by screen resolution (~150 dpi versus printers 2400+ dpi). Patches (MathType, MathML) exist but are inferior to TeX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden formatting commands in word processors
rubrics_metrics.description: Any file produced by a word processor will contain hidden formatting commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cutting and moving pieces of text can carry hidden commands causing formatting issues; moving complex displays may break formatting and waste time fixing them. Because TeX is markup-based, such malady is avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word processors are not universally compatible for math
rubrics_metrics.description: No word processor is universal; all are compatible to a degree, but not in the way that they treat mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaborating across systems using non-TeX word processors can hinder mathematical work; TeX (or variants) is the de facto choice in mathematics for portability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text editor files should be plain ASCII for TeX
rubrics_metrics.description: A file created with a text editor should comprise only the original ASCII code, together with space and line break commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text editors avoid hidden bytes or secondary data; for TeX one should create source with a text editor rather than a word processor to prevent confusing the TeX compiler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use TeX (markup language) rather than a word processor for typesetting mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: TEX is a markup language that gives typesetting and formatting commands, allowing precise positioning (to 10^{-6} inch accuracy) and excellent mathematics typesetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TeX handles spacing/justification automatically, excellent math layout, and portability across platforms. Compile with tex/latex/amstex to produce device-independent dvi files and translate to PostScript/PDF. Learn LaTeX for structure; AMS variants provide journal styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use a word processor to create TeX source files
rubrics_metrics.description: You should not use a word processor to create your TEX source file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hidden binary formatting commands in word-processor files will confuse the TeX compiler and yield incorrect output. Use a plain text editor instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and choose appropriate TeX variant
rubrics_metrics.description: LATEX is a particularly popular form of TEX, favored by publishers; AMS-TEX and other variants exist for discipline-specific needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LATEX steers toward standard formatting; Plain TeX is most flexible. Most mathematicians use TeX/LaTeX; departments typically have support. Start learning gradually—the curve is steep but worthwhile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use TeX-aware preview and print hard copy for final output
rubrics_metrics.description: Preview programs allow viewing document layout for elementary editing, but to view the final output accurately you must print a hard copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screen resolution is limited; previews are helpful but not a substitute for checking printed output, especially for final appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell-checkers: use them but don't over-rely
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell-checkers are highly sophisticated and can catch many typographical errors, but never allow them to lull you into a false sense of security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell-checkers flag non-words but miss real-word errors (e.g., 'unclear' vs 'nuclear', 'weird' vs 'wired'). Ultimate responsibility for correctness lies with the author; continue manual proofreading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use TeX-aware spell-checkers or TeX mode
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use a garden variety spell-checker on a TEX document, it will flag every TeX command and math formula; use a TeX-aware spell-checker (e.g., MicroSpell in 'TEX mode').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TeX mode prevents the spell-checker from treating commands and math as words, avoiding agony when processing TeX source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word counters can detect overused words but can harm creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Word counter tools report word frequencies and can help detect personal foibles (e.g., overusing 'really').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use word-counting software to find overused words, but beware of obsessing—one professional author developed writer's block after overusing software suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare figures on high-quality paper and draw larger than final size
rubrics_metrics.description: Each figure should be on a separate piece of high quality drawing paper and drawn in dense black ink; draw the figures considerably larger than they will appear in the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a proper drawing pen (not ballpoint or pencil). Photographically reducing larger drawings produces sharper, denser pen strokes in print. Keep figures uncluttered, avoid extraneous strokes, and display the message prominently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label figures clearly and reference them in text
rubrics_metrics.description: Each figure should be labeled clearly (e.g., 'Chapter 3 Section 2 Figure 5') and the text should contain a specific reference to each figure by name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give each figure a title and caption (helpful though not mandatory). Do not leave it to the reader to determine which figure goes with which ideas; same applies to tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Import graphics into TeX using floats and includegraphics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \begin{figure} to create a 'float' and \includegraphics[height=..., width=...]{file} plus \caption{...}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Floats let TeX place figures for best fit. Provide the graphics file (e.g., .eps) and specify size. Some TeX variants support specific graphics languages; consult documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate graphics tools and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Use graphics packages (Adobe Illustrator, CorelDRAW, xfig) or plotting software; output formats include .pdf, .bmp, .eps, .ps, .wmf, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the proper tool for the job: vector drawing tools for simple shapes/labels (triangles/rectangles) and plotting software (Mathematica/Mathematicar) for complex function graphs. Ensure your TeX setup understands the graphics language; use Ghostscript to translate if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the right tool: plotting vs drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Mathematica (Mathematicar) for graphing complicated functions quickly; use Corel DRAW or Illustrator for simple diagrams and manual labeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated plotting tools excel at complex plots but may be cumbersome for simple labeled diagrams; choose the tool that fits the task to save time and get clearer results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of font choices and publisher needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Different fonts have different technical qualities (e.g., MathTime vs Computer Modern) and publishers may have preferences (AMS fonts, blackboard bold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some fonts improve readability and symbol distinctness (Spivak's MathTime addresses indistinguishable Greek, parentheses, root signs). AMS provides style files and fonts to match journal requirements; consider publisher/JOURNAL styles when preparing manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypertext can enhance electronic documents
rubrics_metrics.description: With hypertext, words or phrases can be accented and clicked to jump to definitions, lexicons, references, home pages, or animated graphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hypertext to make electronic documents navigable — click to jump to definitions, references, or related material. Hypertext opens new possibilities for reading and interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand implications of electronic journals and Open Access
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic journals execute all transactions over the Internet; Open Access (OA) means anyone can read articles without paying a subscription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OA journals may charge authors substantial fees (often thousands of dollars) if commercially published; NIH mandates OA for NIH-funded research. OA can democratize access but may incentivize dishonest publishers to accept substandard papers for revenue—be cautious about journal quality.
